opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Right now the internet is organized around destinations. You open a browser, go to a site, navigate its interface, fill out forms, copy something from one tab, and paste it into another. You're doing the orchestration yourself, and every app has its own logic you have to learn.

A task-oriented operating system flips that. The unit of interaction stops being the app or the website and becomes the thing you're trying to get done. You say, "I need to plan a trip to Tokyo in March that fits my calendar and budget," and the system figures out which services to touch, what to compare, and when to come back and ask you a question. The internet becomes more of a backend than a place you visit.

A few things change because of that. First, interfaces become ephemeral. Instead of every company designing one static UI for millions of people, the model can generate the right interface for this task, right now. Maybe that's a little comparison table, maybe a calendar view, maybe a single confirm button. I find that really exciting from a design perspective, because the canvas becomes dynamic.

Second, the relationship between humans and models becomes more collaborative and asynchronous. You delegate something, the model works on it in the background, and it surfaces when it needs your judgment. So a big design question becomes: when should the model interrupt you? How does it show its work so you can trust it? How do you steer it midway? Those are the hard problems, more than raw capability.

Third, it changes the economics of the web. If agents do most of the browsing, websites are optimizing for being legible and useful to models, not just to human eyeballs and ad impressions. That's a big shift, and I don't think anyone fully knows how it shakes out.

The thing I'd caution is that we shouldn't take the human out of the loop entirely. Much of the value of the internet is serendipity: stumbling onto something you didn't know you wanted. A purely task-oriented system could make life efficient but narrow. So the best version, I think, keeps room for exploration and creativity. The model handles the tedious parts and gives you more room for curiosity, rather than less.

r001.rationale: The response suggests people will interact with tasks instead of visiting websites, but it does not say this will happen within a few years.

r002.rationale: It describes a model handling the task by choosing and using services, making AI the intermediary between people and the internet.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the browser stops being the center of gravity. Right now, the internet is organized around destinations. You open a tab, you go to a website, you navigate someone else's interface, and you do the work of stitching together whatever you were actually trying to accomplish. The task lived in your head, and the computer just gave you a bunch of pages.

A task-oriented operating system flips that. You start with the intent. "Book a trip for my parents in March, they don't like early flights, and my mom needs an aisle seat." And the system is the thing that goes out to the internet, reads the pages, fills the forms, compares options, and comes back with something that's already shaped around you. The websites become more like APIs or data sources than places you visit. You might never see most of them.

What I find really interesting is what that does to the design of the web itself. For twenty years, sites were optimized for human eyeballs and attention, which is where a lot of the dark patterns come from. If the primary visitor is an agent acting on behalf of a person, a lot of that incentive structure just stops working. You can't upsell a model with a pop-up. So I think we'll see a split: a layer of the internet built for agents to read and act on, and a much smaller, more intentional layer that's built for humans to actually experience, because they want to, not because they have to.

The other piece is that access becomes much more about delegation and trust than about navigation. The question stops being "do I know where to find this" and becomes "what am I comfortable letting this system do for me, and how does it show its work." I think that's healthy, honestly. It makes a lot of the internet more accessible to people who were never going to learn fifteen different interfaces. But it also means the OS has a huge amount of responsibility, because it's now mediating almost everything you do online. Getting the transparency and the controllability right is going to matter more than any individual capability.

r001.rationale: The response suggests people may rarely visit websites directly, but it does not predict fewer clicks within a few years.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent or model acting on the person’s behalf to read pages, fill forms, and compare options, clearly making AI a mediator of internet access.

astra-6.text:
I think it shifts the starting point from “Which app or website do I need?” to “What am I trying to do?” Today, you translate your goal into a sequence of actions: open a browser, search, compare information, move between tabs. In a task-oriented operating system, you could express the goal, and the system would help coordinate those steps across different services.

So the internet might feel less like a collection of destinations and more like a set of capabilities you can access through a conversation. But I don’t think that means browsing disappears. Sometimes you want to explore without a specific outcome in mind. The interesting design question is how you move between delegating a task and taking control yourself—seeing what the system found, changing direction, or deciding that you want to do part of it manually.

r001.rationale: The response says access may shift from websites to conversational capabilities, but it does not predict fewer website clicks within a few years.

r002.rationale: The response describes a system coordinating steps across services, but does not say that AI models will mediate internet access.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the starting point. Today, you open a browser, choose a website, and figure out how to get something done. With a task-oriented operating system, you start with what you want to accomplish, and the system helps coordinate the steps across different applications.

So if you’re planning a trip, you might describe your constraints and preferences instead of opening a bunch of tabs and manually comparing everything. The interesting design question becomes: when should the system act, and when should it bring you in to make a decision? You still need to understand what it found, what tradeoffs it made, and what you’re committing to.

I don’t think browsing goes away. Sometimes exploring is the point—you don’t know what you want yet. But for tasks where you do know the outcome you’re looking for, the internet could feel much less like navigating individual destinations and much more like working with something that helps you get there.

r001.rationale: It suggests less navigation between individual destinations for goal-oriented tasks, but does not clearly predict fewer website clicks within a few years.

r002.rationale: It describes a task-oriented system coordinating steps across applications, but does not say that AI models will mediate people’s access to the internet.
